title: Luke 19
description: Luke 19 in the Liberation and Inclusion Translation (LIT).
paragraphs: 1 After he went into Jericho, he started to travel through it. 2 A man named Zakkaia was there. He was a lead tax collector,b and he was wealthy. 3 He was trying to see who Jesus was, but he was unable to see from among the crowd because he was short. 4 He ran ahead to the front and climbed a sycamore tree so he could see him because Jesusc was going to pass through there.
5 When Jesus came to the spot, he looked up and said to him, “Zakkai, hurry and come down, because it’s essentiald for me to stay at your house today.” 6 He hurried down and welcomed Jesus joyfully.
7 When everyone saw it, they began to criticize it, saying, “He went inside to lodge with a man who deviates!”e
8 Standing up,f Zakkai said to the Lord, “Sir, look, I’m giving half of what I possess to people in poverty, and if I’ve extorted anything from anyone, I’m giving it back four times as much!”g
9 Then Jesus said to him, “Today, restorationh has come to this house, because he too is a son of Abraham! 10 After all, the Son of Humanityi came to seek and restore what has been lost.”j

11 Since the people were listening to these things, he went on and told a parable because he was close to Jerusalem and because they thought God’s Reign was going to become immediately apparent. 12 Therefore, he said, “One elite-born person went to a distant region to obtain the right to reignk for himself and return. 13 He called ten of the people enslaved to him and gave them ten minas.l He told them, ‘Carry on business until I come back.’ 14 However, his citizens set about repudiatingm him and sent a delegation after him who would say, ‘We do not want this person to reign over us.’ 15 When he returned after obtaining the right to reign, he summoned the enslaved workers to whom he had given the money to learn what profit they had made. 16 The first one approached, saying, ‘Sir, your mina made ten more.’ 17 The elite-born personn told him, ‘Well done, you usefulo slave! Because you were faithful with the least important thing, you are to have authority over ten cities!’ 18 Then the second one came, saying, ‘Sir, your mina made five minas.’ 19 So he told that one, ‘You are to be over five cities!’ 20 Then the other one came, saying, ‘Sir, here is your mina that I kept reserved in a cloth. 21 After all, I was afraid of you because you are a harsh person. You pick up what you did not set down,p and you harvest what you did not plant.’ 22 The elite-born person said to him, ‘I will judge you according to your own mouth, you worthlessq slave! You already knew that I am a harsh person, did you? That I pick up what I didn’t set down and harvest what I didn’t plant? 23 What was the reason you didn’t depositr my money in the bank? Then when I came, I would have collected it with interest.’ 24 He told those standing by, ‘Take the mina away from him and give it to the one who has ten minas!’ 25 They said to him, ‘Sir, he already has ten minas!’ 26 ‘I’m telling you that everyone who has something will be given more, but anyone who doesn’t have anything, even what they have will be taken away. 27 Moreover, bring my enemies here, who didn’t want me to reign over them, and slaughter them in front of me!’”

28 After saying these things, he started on ahead, going ups to Jerusalem. 29 As he was approaching Bethphage and Bethany, at the Mount of Olives, he sent two of the students, 30 saying, “Go to the village up ahead. As you enter, you’ll find tied there a colt that no one has ever ridden. Untie it and bring it back. 31 If anyone says to you, ‘Why are you untying it?’ answer like this: ‘Its mastert needs it.’”

32 After they left, the ones who were sent found it just as he had told them. 33 As they were untying the colt, its ownersu said to them, “Why are you untying the colt?” 34 So they said, “Because its master needs it.” 35 They brought it back to Jesus and tossed their cloaks onto the colt and helped Jesus get on it. 36 As he was going along, they spread their cloaks on the road.

37 Right as he approached, coming down from the Mount of Olives, the whole large crowd of students began rejoicing and praising God with a loud voice for all the powerful acts they had seen. 38 They said,

The one who is coming has God’s favor,v

The king in the name of the Lord!

Well-beingw in the heavens

And honorx in the highest places!
39 But some of the Pharisees among the crowd said to him, “Teacher, reprimand your students!” 40 He answered, “I’m telling you, if they go silent, the stones will cry out!”

41 When Jesusy got closer and saw the city, he wept over it, 42 saying “If only you—yes, you—had known on this day what makes for well-being!z But as it is,aa it’s hidden from your eyes. 43 That’s why the days will arrive upon you when those hostile to youbb will surround you, build a siege embankment around you and press in from all sides. 44 They will demolish you and dash your children to the ground within you, and not a stone within you will be left on another because you didn’t recognize the moment of God’scc coming to look after you.”dd

45 When he entered the sacred grounds, Jesusee began driving out the people who were selling things, 46 saying to them, “It is written, ‘My house will be called a house of prayer,’ff but you are making it a ‘stronghold for brigands!’”gg

47 Then he began teaching each day in the sacred grounds. The lead priests, the Scripture scholars, and the foremost among the people began looking to kill him, 48 but they did not find a way to do it because all the people hung on his every word.hh

footnotes.label: a
footnotes.html: Zakkay is the Hebrew name underlying the Greek Zakchaios. Many names were de-Judaized through layers of translation and tradition, making their original Hebrew roots less visible to modern readers. The familiar English form Zacchaeus descends through Latin from the Greek. Zakkay appears in Ezra and Nehemiah, rooted in the Hebrew zakak, meaning “pure” or “clean.”

footnotes.label: b
footnotes.html: The Greek word architelones appears only here. It seems to refer not only to a tax collector but someone who supervised a network of tax collectors under him, contracting with them to collect on his behalf. Every tax collector was already seen as a traitor, extracting money from their own people for the occupying Romans. Zakkai multiplied this offense by as many people as he had working under him, plus enriching himself on others’ labor in collecting. His extreme wealth came from both layers of extraction.

footnotes.label: c
footnotes.html: The name “Jesus” is added for clarity.

footnotes.label: d
footnotes.html: Or, ‘it must be’ or ‘it must happen’ or ‘it has to be’ or ‘it’s an obligation’ or ‘it’s determined’

footnotes.label: e
footnotes.html: The word in Greek here is hamartolos, traditionally translated ‘sinner.’ The word, however, is not a noun but an adjective, describing something about someone, not labeling the whole person. The actual meaning is an archery term for missing the target; it’s a metaphor. It evokes an image of veering off course, ending up at an unintended location. It is used regarding many situations, including harmful behavior, disregarding responsibilities as a people or individual called to a specific purpose, and even having chronic illness or debilitating injuries or cultural identities that prohibit one from full participation in temple worship according to the Torah, which is not implied to be wrongdoing but simply not aligned with Torah. Importantly, the word also functioned as a social label, marking out a class of people treated as rejected and ostracized, whose exclusion the insiders who applied the label regarded as deserved. In the Gospels this reflects the social perspective of the surrounding culture, the verdict of insiders against those they reject, rather than an evaluation the narrative itself endorses.

footnotes.label: f
footnotes.html: Or ‘stood still’

footnotes.label: g
footnotes.html: Exodus 22:1 states that theft of a sheep requires paying back four sheep as restitution. However, Zakkai is doing something interesting here, intentionally shouldering the burden of the harshest penalty, plus giving away half his wealth, which was entirely voluntary. The Torah instruction specifically regarding someone who confesses fraud, extortion, or robbery is different than someone who was convicted of theft. Leviticus 6:1-5 and Numbers 5:6-7 instruct people who confess their wrongdoing against another to pay back what they deprived the injured party plus an additional twenty percent. So Zakkai confesses but assigns himself the convicted thief’s penalty instead. Given the two layers of extraction his position involved (see note on verse 2), getting rich off other’s labor is theft whether or not any law names it that way, and Zakkai acknowledges his profits as exactly that, choosing to pay the most restitution possible for the wrongs.

footnotes.label: h
footnotes.html: Traditionally, ‘salvation.’ This word carries a meaning of any kind of action to prevent or repair harm. Appropriate translations could be ‘liberation,’ ‘restoration,’ ‘rescue,’ ‘healing,’ ‘preservation,’ or ‘protection.’

footnotes.label: i
footnotes.html: Reference to Ezekiel—“Son of Man” was how Ezekiel referred to himself—and to Daniel 7:13-27. This is one of the loftiest titles Jesus could have used for himself and likely played a key role in accusations against him of attempting to usurp the royal throne. At the same time, though Daniel 7:13-14 connects the “one like a son of humanity” to a kingship with all peoples serving him and that his kingship shall never be destroyed, continuing to verse 27 is the parallel verse that explains it further, and it asserts that “the greatness of the kingdoms under the whole heaven shall be given to the people” as an everlasting kingdom. It also left Jesus with deniability, since he could also claim just to be calling himself a prophet in the tradition of Ezekiel.

footnotes.label: j
footnotes.html: The traditional translation is “the lost,” but in English that sounds like a class of people who are lost, which is not what the Greek describes. To point that way, the form would be masculine plural. Instead it is neuter and singular, a perfect participle: not “lost people” but “the thing that has been lost,” and lost in a way that persists. Luke has already spent significant time on lost things in chapter 15, where what is lost (the sheep, the coin, the younger son), is in every case something that already belonged to the one searching, sought precisely because it was already theirs and not because it was an outside category to be brought in. That reframes this verse. Traditional theology has read “the lost” as the mass of the population, but the grammar points instead to a single thing belonging to Zakkai himself: his identity as a son of Abraham. What has been lost seems to be the chosenness of that lineage, the promise that through Abraham’s descendants belonging and well-being would be extended to everyone. The framing is that even the most traitorous figure, one who harms the general population, can in fact be restored to the community where he belongs.

footnotes.label: k
footnotes.html: The word basileia is traditionally translated ‘kingdom,’ which works in some contexts. It is also the word rendered ‘reign’ in the phrase ‘God’s Reign.’ Here it is not indicating a territory to rule but the very right to rule. It seems to reference the Roman prerogative of designating a region’s ruler, and it is often understood as an allusion to Herod Archelaus, son of Herod the Great. After his father’s death Archelaus was pressed to take the royal title but deferred, declining it until he could sail to Rome and have his claim confirmed by Caesar amid a contested succession. Augustus granted him Judea but withheld the kingship, naming him ethnarch instead. The parable’s elite-born person, who returns having secured the basileia he traveled for, echoes this world of rule dispensed through imperial endorsement.

footnotes.label: l
footnotes.html: A mina was 100 denarii, and each denarius was the subsistence wage for one day of labor.

footnotes.label: m
footnotes.html: Traditionally, ‘hated.’ ‘Set about repudiating him’ renders the Greek miseo in the imperfect tense, indicating ongoing past action or the beginning of an ongoing action. The verb spans active postures of hostility and, in many Semitic contexts, the withdrawal or reversal of loyalty. Here the citizens are not expressing emotional hatred but formally rejecting the person’s authority, refusing him as their ruler, as the rest of the verse makes explicit: they send a delegation declaring they will not have this man reign over them. The verb names a repudiation of allegiance, a public disowning of rule, not personal animosity. The scene closely tracks the historical embassy of Judeans to Rome opposing the kingship of Herod Archelaus.

footnotes.label: n
footnotes.html: “Elite-born person” is added for clarity, where the Greek literally says, ‘he.’

footnotes.label: o
footnotes.html: In Greek, agathos generally means “good,” but more often implying what is beneficial, useful, or constructive, rather than merely “good” in an abstract or moral sense. In literature outside the Bible, agathos often describes things that serve a beneficial purpose or contribute positively to well-being. This meaning is also reflected in the Septuagint, where agathos describes both moral goodness and practical benefits.

footnotes.label: p
footnotes.html: The words ‘pick up’ and ‘set down’ are very literal translations and often what they meant, but it could also be used to refer to depositing and withdrawing from a bank.

footnotes.label: q
footnotes.html: The Greek term poneros in Greek extends beyond “evil,” often signifying something burdensome, troublesome, or marked by hardship, with roots in ponos—“toil” or “pain.” In secular Greek literature of the time, poneros frequently describes unfavorable or difficult conditions, such as physical ailments or adverse circumstances, emphasizing hardship without implying inherent moral corruption. Similarly, in the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible), poneros is often used to describe harm or undesirable situations without a moral judgment. The Cambridge Greek Lexicon lists “worthless” as one of the recognized uses, as a description of something or someone that does not provide a benefit or actively increases hardship.

footnotes.label: r
footnotes.html: The word here is didomi, which is different from the word for ‘set down’ in verse 21.

footnotes.label: s
footnotes.html: No matter the starting point, going to the temple is always described as ‘going up’ in scripture. It’s not about location on the map or elevation; it’s about it having the highest spiritual and religious significance.

footnotes.label: t
footnotes.html: The word kurios is traditionally translated ‘lord,’ but it was used in a variety of ways. Here, it is referring specifically to the person who has authority over the colt, and it would be odd for an English speaker to refer to the owner of livestock as the livestock’s lord. ‘Master’ is used here to differentiate the role Jesus has in contrast with the role of the multiple kurioi, or ‘owners,’ that are discussed in the upcoming paragraph in verse 33, though it is the same Greek word.

footnotes.label: u
footnotes.html: This is the plural form of the word kurios, which is usually translated as ‘lord’ but has other uses depending on context. It’s the same word that is translated as ‘master’ in reference to Jesus in verses 31 and 34.

footnotes.label: v
footnotes.html: The word ‘God’s’ has been added for clarity. The traditional translation of eulogemenos is ‘blessed is’ or ‘is blessed.’ However, the Greek is a passive participle in the perfect tense, indicating past, completed action. The English word ‘blessed’ gets confusing as it translates two unrelated Greek words with different meanings and has acquired sentimental meaning that is not part of the Greek word’s significance. The word here means something like ‘praise’ or ‘speak well of’ or more relevant to this passage, to pronounce a positive future of well being or purpose over someone. In this case, it’s the completed pronouncement of the present purpose of being “king in the name of the Lord.”

footnotes.label: w
footnotes.html: “Well-being” translates the Greek word eirene, which is often rendered “peace.” But like the Hebrew shalom, it implies more than emotional calm. It refers to being restored, healed, whole, reconnected—to God, to community, and to one’s full human dignity.

footnotes.label: x
footnotes.html: Traditionally, ‘glory’

footnotes.label: y
footnotes.html: The name ‘Jesus’ is added for clarity.

footnotes.label: z
footnotes.html: “Well-being” translates the Greek word eirene, which is often rendered “peace.” But like the Hebrew shalom, it implies more than emotional calm. It refers to being restored, healed, whole, reconnected—to God, to community, and to one’s full human dignity.

footnotes.label: aa
footnotes.html: Most translations say, ‘but now’ as if to imply the situation has changed and it’s too late. The Greek nun de is a specific construction that follows the Greek ei (‘if’). In that construction it is not about time but about the fact of how things were in contrast with the imagined condition described by the ‘if’ clause.

footnotes.label: bb
footnotes.html: Traditionally, ‘enemies.’ The rendering ‘those hostile to you’ clarify that word indicates ‘enemies’ refer to people who are hostile toward the person in view, not people toward whom the person is hostile. One’s enemies are not the ones a person hates or harms but the ones doing the harm.

footnotes.label: cc
footnotes.html: The word ‘God’s’ is added for clarity.

footnotes.label: dd
footnotes.html: The phrase ‘coming to look after you’ translates the Greek episkopes, the noun form of the verb episkeptomai, ‘to look in on, attend to, come to the aid of.’ It is a compound of skopeo (to look at, watch over) and the prefix epi- (upon), so the image is a looking-upon that is about ensuring someone is cared for, not an inspection to find fault. The traditional ‘visitation’ loses part of this, addressing only the idea of coming. Within Luke, the word always marks care arriving, not a judgment being handed down. It appears in Luke 1:68, where God ‘looked in on the people’ and purchased them from enslavement; in Luke 1:78, where the dawn will ‘look in on us from the heights’; and in Luke 7:16, in the crowd’s acclamation after Jesus raises someone from the dead, where they name him a great prophet and declare that God ‘has come to look after the people.’

footnotes.label: ee
footnotes.html: The name ‘Jesus’ is added for clarity.

footnotes.label: ff
footnotes.html: Citation of Isaiah 56:7, but this story in Luke cannot be rightly understood without looking at the whole of Isaiah 56. Undoubtedly, Jesus was referring to the ideas in the whole chapter (and even the following chapters), including the instruction to promote justice, to welcome foreigners and eunuchs (who were traditionally excluded from temple worship) and the indictment that the authorities are each ‘looking for monetary gain.’ Jesus identifies the current situation with chapters 56-58 and is doing the work to usher in what is described in chapters 59-62 and beyond.

footnotes.label: gg
footnotes.html: The phrase here is from Jeremiah 7:11, but context of the whole chapter is in view where Jeremiah speaks on behalf of the LORD telling people to change their ways and start doing justice for each other, stop oppressing immigrants, orphans, and widows (who would have had no way to earn a living), stop killing innocent people, stop paying allegiance to gods whose ways were in contradiction to all these teachings. The entirety of Jeremiah 7 (also 8 and 9) is relevant and includes the prediction that their fate will be as the Valley of Ben Hinnom and death and the destruction of the temple (which happened about 40 years later in AD 70). See footnotes for Matthew 5:22 and Matthew 5:29.

footnotes.label: hh
footnotes.html: Literally, ‘hung on what they heard’
